title: Victory over death
hookLine: some early Christian writers saw the cross as Christ defeating death and evil

lines: ADAM AND EVE PULLED BY THE WRISTS.
cards: A gate lies flat on the ground, broken in two, its bolts scattered like dropped keys. A figure in white stands on the pieces, pulling an old man and an old woman up out of their graves by the wrists.
That's the Anastasis, the resurrection icon of the Eastern churches. Other Easter icons show the women at the empty tomb.

This one shows a rescue: the prison of the dead smashed open, and Adam and Eve, the man and woman from the garden, hauled out. Day three hundred two asked why the cross. Now, a bigger question: what did it actually do?
Christians give more than one answer, and some hold several together. Today's answer is a battle, and a winner.

teach.b: The Latin name is Christus Victor: Christ the victor. In this picture, humanity is held hostage.

teach.h: FREED FROM THE FEAR OF DEATH.
teach.b: Death, sin and the devil have us, and nobody breaks out from the inside. So God comes in.
Hebrews says Christ shared our flesh and blood "that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil."
And why it matters: to set free those who "through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage." The enemy isn't only death. It's the fear of death, leaning on a whole life.
Paul's letter to the Colossians uses the picture of a Roman triumph, a victory parade: Christ "having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it."
The powers that seemed to win on Good Friday are paraded as the beaten side. Some early Christian writers told it almost like a trick.
Death swallowed Jesus the way it swallows everyone, found it had swallowed life itself, and couldn't keep it down. Gregory of Nyssa even pictured a fishhook hidden in bait.

teach.h: O DEATH, WHERE IS THY STING?
teach.b: Then Paul, in his first letter to Corinth, gets to taunt: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" You can hear it at Easter in the Orthodox hymn of Christ trampling down death by death.
Churches can hold this picture alongside others. This one is simple: the cross was a fight, and the fight is over.

how: In Orthodox churches the Easter hymn proclaiming Christ trampling down death by death is sung again and again through the Easter season, and the resurrection icon shows Christ raising Adam and Eve from the broken gates of death; Protestant and Catholic Christians also sing and preach this victory, especially at Easter.

games.q: you're painting the Anastasis, the resurrection icon. which moment does it show?
o: an empty tomb with folded cloths.
Christ standing on broken gates, pulling Adam and Eve up out of their graves.
the disciples hiding behind a locked door.
games.why: the Anastasis paints the rescue: death's prison smashed and the first humans hauled out. victory, not just absence.

practice: Think of something that has held you hostage, a fear, a habit, a grief, a voice that says you're finished, and give it a plain name. Picture it as that broken gate, flat on the ground.
If you pray, name it to Christ as one thing he has defeated; if you don't, notice what it would feel like for that thing to have no last word.

wordCard.voice: Christus Victor. Latin for Christ the victor: the cross and the empty tomb as a battle won over death, sin and evil.

orig.note: Greek: victory, the word behind "O grave, where is thy victory?"

carryVoice: Your line: death is defeated. The gate of death lies broken on the ground. See you tomorrow.
